--- title: "Warum das Einkommen logarithmieren?" subtitle: "Regressionsanalysen" author: "Daria Tisch" format: revealjs: theme: default slide-number: true code-fold: true echo: true execute: warning: false message: false --- ## 1. Das Problem: Die Verteilung des Einkommens {.scrollable} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(stevedata) library(tidyverse) library(sjPlot) library(gridExtra) df_clean <- stevedata::gss_wages %>% filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(realrinc), realrinc > 0) ``` ::: Einkommen sind typischerweise **rechtsschief** verteilt: Wenige Top-Verdiener ziehen den Mittelwert nach rechts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_real = ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = realrinc)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Rohes Einkommen", x = "USD", y = "Häufigkeit") p_log = ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = log(realrinc))) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "forestgreen", color = "white") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Logarithmiertes Einkommen", x = "log(USD)", y = "Häufigkeit") grid.arrange(p_real, p_log, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](quarto_presentation_files/figure-html/fig-distributions-1.png){#fig-distributions width=960} ::: ::: ## 2. Lineares vs. Log-lineares Modell {.scrollable} Vergleich der Regression von Einkommen auf das Alter ($\text{Einkommen} \sim \text{Alter}$). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_linear <- lm(realrinc ~ age, data = df_clean) m_log <- lm(log(realrinc) ~ age, data = df_clean) ``` ::: ### Lineares Modell {.scrollable} ```{.r .cell-code} tab_model(m_linear, show.aic = TRUE) ``` `````{=html}
  R's income in constant$
Predictors Estimates CI p
(Intercept) 8628.73 7720.61 – 9536.85 <0.001
Age of respondent 334.33 313.27 – 355.39 <0.001
Observations 37825
R2 / R2 adjusted 0.025 / 0.025
AIC 882587.716
````` ## 2. Das Log-lineare Modell im Vergleich {.scrollable} ### Log-lineares Modell ($\ln(\text{Einkommen}) \sim \text{Alter}$) {.scrollable} ```{.r .cell-code} tab_model(m_log, show.aic = TRUE) ``` `````{=html}
  R's income in constant$
Predictors Estimates CI p
(Intercept) 8.93 8.90 – 8.97 <0.001
Age of respondent 0.01 0.01 – 0.02 <0.001
Observations 37825
R2 / R2 adjusted 0.030 / 0.029
AIC 834221.357
````` ## 3. Das Heteroskedastie-Problem (Residuenplot) {.scrollable} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df_clean <- df_clean %>% mutate( fitted_lin = fitted(m_linear), resid_lin = residuals(m_linear), fitted_log = fitted(m_log), resid_log = residuals(m_log) ) p1 <- ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = fitted_lin, y = resid_lin)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "darkred") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Lineares Modell", subtitle = "Trichterform (Heteroskedastie)", x = "Vorhergesagt", y = "Residuen") p2 <- ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = fitted_log, y = resid_log)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "darkgreen") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Log-lineares Modell", subtitle = "Konstantere Streuung", x = "Vorhergesagt (log)", y = "Residuen") grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](quarto_presentation_files/figure-html/fig-residuals-1.png){#fig-residuals width=960} ::: ::: ## 4. Interpretation des Koeffizienten {.scrollable} Wie interpretieren wir den Effekt des Alters im Log-Modell? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} beta_age <- coef(m_log)["age"] # Faustregel-Interpretation prozent_faustregel <- beta_age * 100 # Exakte Interpretation: (exp(beta) - 1) * 100 prozent_exakt <- (exp(beta_age) - 1) * 100 ``` ::: - **Koeffizient (**$\beta$): 0.0142 - **Faustregel (**$100 \cdot \beta$): 1.42% pro Lebensjahr - **Exakt (**$(e^\beta - 1) \cdot 100$): 1.43% pro Lebensjahr
